title: Addressing Sleep and Sleepiness In ShifT workers (ASSIST)
official: Clinical and cost-effectiveness of a behavioural sleep intervention for shift work sleep disorder: A randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Shift work can often lead to significant sleep disruption because the work schedule conflicts with the usual time for sleep and can confuse our body clock. When a shift work schedule causes problems with falling asleep, staying asleep, or excessive sleepiness, it is known as shift work disorder (SWD), which can have a major impact on health and well-being. This study aims to compare two different approaches that may help improve sleep in shift workers who experience these difficulties.

Who can participate?
NHS shift workers who meet the criteria for SWD can take part in this study. 

What does the study involve?
Participants' eligibility will be checked in two stages: first through an online questionnaire, and then via a brief online or telephone interview with a member of the research team. If eligible, participants will give their consent and complete online questionnaires on sleep, fatigue, quality of life, mental health, and overall health. They will also complete a sleep diary on a digital sleep app for 14 consecutive days.

Participants will then be randomly assigned to receive either the OxBIS intervention or sleep hygiene education (SHE). The Oxford Behavioural Intervention for Shift work (OxBIS) intervention involves six one-to-one online sessions with a trained facilitator. The sessions will take place 1 to 2 weeks apart and will last about one hour each. Participants in the SHE group will receive a booklet containing information and practical tips to help improve their sleep.

Follow-up assessments will be completed at 13, 26, and 52 weeks after randomisation.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may benefit from improved sleep and from learning more about their sleep and ways to improve it. By taking part, participants will also help researchers understand how to improve sleep problems in people who work shifts, which may benefit others in the future.

No serious risks are expected from taking part in the study. However, some participants may find questions about their sleep or health upsetting. Changes to sleep patterns may also lead to increased sleepiness for a short time. If this happens, participants will be asked to take extra care with activities that require a high level of alertness, such as driving or operating machinery. If participants feel unusually sleepy while working, they will be advised to speak to their line manager or occupational health team.

Where is the study run from?
University of Oxford, UK. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to March 2029.

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Programme Grants for Applied Research, UK.

Who is the main contact?
1. Dr Thava Priya Sugavanam, Programme Manager, Oxford Centre for Diabetes, priya.sugavanam@ocdem.ox.ac.uk
2. Dr Forrest Tin Wai Cheung, Postdoctoral Research Associate, Sir Jules Thorn Sleep and Circadian Neuroscience Institute, forrest.cheung@ndcn.ox.ac.uk
3. Prof Simon D Kyle, Principal investigator, Sir Jules Thorn Sleep and Circadian Neuroscience Institute, simon.kyle@ndcn.ox.ac.uk

Randomisation
Randomisation will be done using a secure, validated, and compliant web-based randomisation system. Allocation will be at a ratio of 1:1 and will be carried out using a non-deterministic minimisation algorithm, stratified by site, sex (male/female/other), age (18-45, >45 yrs), circadia

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
The participant may enter the study if ALL of the following apply:
1.	Willing and able to give informed consent for participation in the study
2.	Aged 18 years or above
3.	Employed by the NHS and working at a participating Trust
4.	Worked non-standard hours (defined as work scheduled after 6 pm or before 7 am) for a minimum of 3 months. 
5.	Meets the DSM-5 criteria for SWD according to self-reported items on the shift work disorder index (SWDI), and a semi-structured interview. This includes the presence of insomnia and/or excessive sleepiness associated with a recurring work schedule outside of standard work hours (minimum of one non-standard shift per week) and that overlaps with or restricts one’s desired sleep schedule. Symptoms must have persisted for 3 months or more and not be better explained by another sleep, medical, or mental disorder.
6.	Has stable internet access and access to technology (e.g., computer, tablet, or smartphone) required to participate in online sessions, if assigned to the intervention arm.

NOTE: Participants will need to have a basic understanding of English to take part in the study, as the intervention and study materials will be delivered in English, and translation services cannot be provided due to the nature of the intervention. As participants will all be NHS staff, we expect this requirement to be met, as a sufficient level of English proficiency is required to undertake NHS roles. We therefore do not anticipate that this requirement will exclude any eligible participants. Hence, this has not been explicitly mentioned as an inclusion/exclusion criterion.
Exclusion criteria:
A participant will not be eligible for the study if ANY of the following apply:
1.	Non-NHS-employed staff (e.g., agency staff, students on placement, honorary staff, contractors)
2.	Not currently working (e.g. long-term absence due to illness, parental leave)
3.	Sleep difficulty better explained by other co-occurring health conditions or factors (e.g., caring responsibilities)
4.	Currently receiving formal psychological treatment for sleep difficulties from a healthcare professional.
5.	Untreated comorbid sleep disorder (e.g., sleep-disordered breathing or sleep-related movement disorder). Comorbid sleep disorders are permitted provided they are actively managed.
6.	Diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment or dementia.
7.	Current suicidal ideation with intent OR attempted suicide within past 6 months
8.	Currently receiving cancer treatment
9.	Planned major surgery during the next 4 months
10.	Taking part in another research study that may affect the outcomes of the present study.
11.	Another member of the same household is taking part in the trial
12.	Previously took part in the OxBIS feasibility study
